questions.explanation: STYLO (Stylosanthes spp., commonly S. hamata, S. scabra, S. guianensis) is a tropical PERENNIAL FORAGE LEGUME native to Brazil, widely used as a range grass and fodder crop. Characteristics: Erect-growing legume, 0.6 to 1.8 m tall. Adapted to tropical climates. Tolerant of low-fertility, acidic soils and poor drainage. Being a legume, fixes atmospheric nitrogen (~50-200 kg N/ha/year), improving soil fertility for companion grasses. Popularly used in silvo-pastoral systems, alley cropping, and reclamation of degraded lands. Improves palatability and protein content of pastures. Uses: Grazing (as pasture, alone or mixed with grasses like Guinea, Setaria). Cut-and-carry green fodder. Green manure. Cover crop in plantations (coconut, arecanut, coffee). The Central Range Management Society and ICAR-IGFRI (Indian Grassland and Fodder Research Institute, Jhansi) promote Stylo for silvi-pastoral rehabilitation of common grazing lands.[cite: 115]

questions.question: The classification of plants into ANNUAL, BIENNIAL, and PERENNIAL is based on which biological aspect?
questions.explanation: ONTOGENY refers to the origin and development of an individual organism, from fertilisation of the egg to maturity - essentially the LIFE HISTORY / LIFE SPAN of the plant. Classification based on ontogeny: ANNUAL: complete life cycle (germination → flowering → seed setting → death) within ONE year/season. Examples: wheat, rice, maize, mustard, most vegetables, cotton (as annual). BIENNIAL: two-year cycle - vegetative in year 1, reproductive in year 2 after vernalization. Examples: sugar beet, beetroot, carrot (seed production), cabbage (seed). PERENNIAL: live and produce for many years. Examples: Napier grass, coconut, mango, tea, sugarcane (ratoon), banana, all fruit trees, alfalfa. Other classification systems: BOTANICAL: based on family (Poaceae, Fabaceae) or morphology. CO2 FIXATION: C3, C4, CAM plants. PHOTOPERIOD: short/long/day-neutral. CROPPING SEASON: kharif, rabi, zaid. END USE: food, fodder, fibre, oilseed, sugar, spice, medicinal. Ontogeny helps in choosing crop rotations, cropping intensity, and long-term farm planning.[cite: 116]

questions.question: The scientific name of HORSE GRAM (a drought-tolerant Indian pulse) is:
questions.explanation: HORSE GRAM (Kulthi, Hurali) — Macrotyloma uniflorum — is a highly drought-tolerant, hardy pulse of Indian origin, grown mainly in dry regions of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, MP, and Chhattisgarh. Formerly classified as Dolichos biflorus, it was renamed to Macrotyloma uniflorum. Common scientific names of Indian pulses: Chickpea: Cicer arietinum. Pigeon pea / Red gram: Cajanus cajan. Black gram / Urd: Vigna mungo. Green gram / Mung: Vigna radiata. Lentil / Masoor: Lens culinaris. Field pea: Pisum arvense. Cowpea / Lobia: Vigna unguiculata. Cluster bean / Guar: Cyamopsis tetragonoloba. Moth bean: Vigna aconitifolia. Rice bean: Vigna umbellata. Fababean: Vicia faba. Common bean / Rajmash: Phaseolus vulgaris. Grasspea / Khesari: Lathyrus sativus. Soybean: Glycine max. Horse gram is nutritionally rich (25% protein) and traditionally used in Ayurveda for kidney stones. It is a good example of a resilient "smart food" being revived under nutritional security programs.[cite: 117]

questions.question: GLUTEN – the protein giving elastic, spongy texture to bread – is found in significant quantities in:
questions.explanation: GLUTEN is a protein complex found naturally in WHEAT, and in smaller amounts in barley and rye. It is composed of two main proteins: GLIADIN (soluble in alcohol) — gives extensibility. GLUTENIN (insoluble) — gives elasticity. When wheat flour is mixed with water and kneaded, gluten forms a stretchy network that traps CO2 (from yeast fermentation or baking powder) — this gives BREAD, cakes, pasta, chapati their characteristic rise and structure. Without gluten, dough would tear easily. Gluten importance in wheat quality: HARD WHEAT (T. aestivum, high protein 12-15%): strong gluten, best for bread. DURUM WHEAT (T. durum, high yellow pigment): for pasta. SOFT WHEAT (low protein 8-10%): for biscuits, cakes. Millets (bajra, ragi, jowar, foxtail etc.) and rice, maize are NATURALLY GLUTEN-FREE. This is why millets are recommended for people with: CELIAC DISEASE (autoimmune gluten intolerance). WHEAT allergy. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity. This is a key reason the UN promoted the International Year of Millets 2023.[cite: 118]

questions.question: Paddy for storage should have its MOISTURE content in the range of:
questions.explanation: For safe storage, PADDY grains should be dried to 10–12% moisture content. Storage at higher moisture (>14%) invites: Fungal / mould growth (Aspergillus, Penicillium) producing aflatoxins. Insect infestation (rice weevil, lesser grain borer). Respiration heat build-up ("hot spots"). Fermentation and quality loss. Discolouration and loss of milling quality. Storage moisture guidelines (%): PADDY: 10–12. WHEAT: 10–12. Maize: 10–12. Oilseeds (mustard, soybean): 6–8 (higher oil deteriorates fast). Pulses: 9–10. Drying steps: 1. Field drying / sun drying on clean floors (traditional). 2. Mechanical drying with heated air (large-scale mills, FCI). Storage structures range from traditional (Bukhari, Morai, Bags in godowns) to modern silos (metal, concrete), FCI godowns, and Cover-and-Plinth (CAP) storage. NABARD's Rural Godown Scheme (Gramin Bhandaran Yojana) supports construction of village-level storage. Post-harvest losses in India are estimated at 5–15% of grain — reducing them is a major policy focus.[cite: 119]
